lead: Today our calendar remembers the prophet Elisha, and the Gospel names him: in his time many in Israel had leprosy, “and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.” Jesus uses Elijah and Elisha to show that God's mercy has always reached beyond the expected boundaries. Paul, for his part, tells the baptized that sin no longer rules them: they are “not under law but under grace.” The key words are grace and mercy without borders.

r.h: Not under law but under grace
set: In Romans 6 Paul answers an objection: if grace abounds where sin abounded, should we go on sinning so that grace may abound all the more (6:1)? His answer is Baptism. We have been buried with Christ by baptism into death, so that we too might walk in newness of life (6:4). Today's verses draw the practical conclusion with a “therefore”: live now as people who have passed from death to life.
str: v. 12: do not let sin reign in your mortal bodies.
v. 13: do not hand your members over to sin; present yourselves and your members to God.
v. 14: sin will have no dominion, because you are under grace.
kw: Paul pictures sin as a king trying to win back a kingdom it has lost. In Baptism the reign of sin is broken, but the believer must refuse to let it return.
The word is often used of weapons. Our hands, eyes and tongue can serve as weapons for wickedness or for righteousness. The body is not the enemy; it is the place where the battle is won.
vv: Therefore, do not let sin exercise dominion in your mortal bodies, to make you obey their passions.
Paul does not say that the baptized will never feel the pull of sin. He says they must not obey it. The struggle remains, but its outcome has changed.
present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and present your members to God as instruments of righteousness.
“Present” is the language of offering. The Christian life is a daily self-offering, the whole person placed in God's hands.
For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
The law showed what is right but could not give the strength to do it. Grace is God's own life in us, and it gives what the law commanded.
ch: The Council of Trent taught, and the Catechism repeats, that after Baptism an inclination to sin called concupiscence remains, left for us to wrestle with; it cannot harm those who do not consent to it and who resist it manfully by the grace of Christ (CCC 1264). The Catechism also teaches that the grace of the Holy Spirit has the power to justify us, cleansing us from our sins and communicating the righteousness of God (CCC 1987–1988). Paul's command is therefore not a heavy burden added to grace. It is grace itself asking for our willing cooperation.

set: Jesus has returned to Galilee “filled with the power of the Spirit” (4:14), and in the synagogue at Nazareth he has read from Isaiah 61. He tells his own townspeople, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21). At first they speak well of him; then they ask, “Is not this Joseph's son?” Jesus answers with a proverb, “no prophet is accepted in the prophet's hometown” (4:24), and then with two examples from Israel's own Scriptures.

The first example is Elijah, sent in a time of famine to a widow of Zarephath in the land of Sidon (1 Kings 17:8–16). The second is Elisha, who healed Naaman, the commander of the army of Aram, when he washed seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:1–14). Both were foreigners; both received God's gift through a prophet of Israel.
str: vv. 25–26: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath.
v. 27: Elisha and Naaman the Syrian.
vv. 28–29: the synagogue's anger; they try to throw him from the hill.
v. 30: Jesus passes through the midst of them.
kw: 1 Kings 18:1 speaks of “the third year”. Luke here, and James 5:17, give three years and a half, a figure that seems to have become traditional. Half of seven, it was also a symbol of a time of trial.
Luke's word for the healing of leprosy. It means more than a cure of the skin: it restores the person to the community and to worship.
vv: yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon.
“Was sent” points to God as the one who sends. The prophet goes where God directs, and God directs him to a foreign widow.
There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.

Naaman was a commander of a hostile army, and at first he was offended at being told simply to wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:11–12). Yet humility and obedience healed him. Jesus' hearers knew the story well; what stung was its point.
But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.

Luke does not explain how. The hour of Jesus' death has not yet come, and it will be in Jerusalem, not on a hill at Nazareth. His “way” is the journey that Luke will follow to the cross and the resurrection.
ch: Luke's Gospel and its second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, show the good news going from Israel to the nations. Today's Gospel is a first sign of that movement, told not to reject Israel but to show the wideness of God's mercy, which Israel's own prophets already knew. St Ambrose, explaining the sacraments to the newly baptized, saw in Naaman's washing in the Jordan a figure of Baptism: it is not the water by itself that cleanses but the word of God and the grace of Christ (On the Mysteries, in substance). The anger at Nazareth belongs to one town and one moment; the Church never reads it as a judgment on the Jewish people, from whom Jesus came and among whom he preached (Nostra Aetate 4).

qa: Why were the people of Nazareth so angry?

They had heard of the wonders Jesus did at Capernaum and expected him to do the same for his own town (4:23). Instead he reminded them that God had once passed over many in Israel to help a foreign widow and a foreign general. It is a hard word for any community that thinks it has a special claim on God. Luke is not blaming a people; he is warning every hearer, Christians included, against thinking that grace is owed to us.
rite: Our Church keeps today the memory of Elisha the Prophet. He asked Elijah for “a double share of your spirit” (2 Kings 2:9), and his ministry was rich in signs of God's care: oil that did not fail for a poor widow, a child raised to life, a foreign commander healed in the Jordan. Scripture adds that a dead man came to life when his body touched Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:21), and the Church has seen in this a sign that God honours the bodies of his saints. On his day we ask for the same humility that healed Naaman, and for the courage to bring God's mercy to those whom others pass by.
study: Paul tells me to present my members to God as instruments of righteousness. What will I do today with my hands, my eyes and my tongue?
Naaman almost refused healing because the remedy seemed too simple. Is there a simple means of grace, such as Confession or daily prayer, that I neglect?
